reason: The sources provide enough factual claims and details to construct a short narrative about the Franklin expedition.
story: In May 1845, British polar explorer Sir John Franklin led 129 men aboard the HMS Erebus and HMS Terror to find the Northwest Passage. Equipped with innovative steam engines and three years of provisions, the ships vanished into the Canadian Arctic. Trapped by thick multi-year ice near King William Island in 1846, the expedition endured bitter cold and dwindling supplies. Franklin died in June 1847. By April 1848, the 105 surviving crew members abandoned their icebound ships and attempted a desperate 400-kilometer march south toward the Back River. None survived. Decades later, oral histories from local Inuit and grim archaeological evidence revealed scurvy, disease, and starvation, leading to desperation and cannibalism. In 2014 and 2016, modern underwater searches finally located the remarkably preserved wrecks of Erebus and Terror, solving one of maritime history's greatest mysteries.
angle: The discovery of HMS Terror in pristine condition with its hatches closed and anchor deployed suggests surviving sailors may have re-boarded and sailed the ship south before it finally sank.

claims.claim: Sir John Franklin departed England in May 1845 with 129 officers and men.
The expedition sailed aboard two ships, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror.
Both ships became icebound in Victoria Strait near King William Island in September 1846.
Sir John Franklin died on June 11, 1847.
The surviving crew abandoned Erebus and Terror on April 22, 1848.
A total of 105 surviving souls set out to march toward Back's Fish River on April 26, 1848.
John Rae reported Inuit accounts of starvation and cannibalism among the dying sailors in 1854.
Lieutenant William Hobson found the Victory Point note in a cairn on King William Island in May 1859.
Parks Canada located the wreck of HMS Erebus in 2014 in Queen Maud Gulf.
The Arctic Research Foundation found the remarkably preserved wreck of HMS Terror in Terror Bay in 2016.
Three crew members died during the first winter of 1845-46 and were buried on Beechey Island.
Archaeological excavations found cut marks on bones, supporting allegations of cannibalism.

disputed: Whether lead poisoning from poorly soldered food tins was the primary cause of debilitation or if zinc deficiency and tuberculosis played a larger role should be attributed as a scientific debate in the script.
Inuit accounts suggesting some survivors re-manned a ship and sailed it south past 1848 should be attributed as oral history or legend.
The exact cause of Sir John Franklin's death on June 11, 1847, remains unknown and should be left unstated.
